analysis.one_liner: Repeals the requirement that federal construction contractors pay locally prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal Davis-Bacon prevailing wage rules never got a committee vote; it was referred to the Senate HELP Committee on January 30, 2017 and died there when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires companies working on federally financed construction to pay workers the locally prevailing wage for their trade. This bill would erase that requirement entirely, and void every other law's reference to it [S2] [S3]. That would let contractors on federal projects pay whatever the market alone forces, which in practice means lower pay for construction workers and lower labor costs for the companies. The bill never advanced past its committee referral [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Federal construction contractors, especially nonunion firms that compete mainly on price, would gain the ability to cut labor costs on public buildings and public works. Proponents also argue taxpayers would save on project costs because prevailing wage rules raise the price of federal construction.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals subchapter IV of chapter 31 of title 40, the Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirements, so contractors on federally financed or assisted construction, alteration, and repair would no longer have to pay locally prevailing wages [S2] [S3].
Voids every reference in other laws to Davis-Bacon wage requirements, removing the prevailing wage floor from federally assisted projects beyond direct federal contracts as well [S2] [S3].
Takes effect 30 days after enactment but does not disturb contracts already in existence or bids already outstanding at that point [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federal projects would bear the cost: the wage floor tied to local prevailing rates would disappear, and where the market pays less, their pay would fall. Union building trades that depend on prevailing wage standards would lose leverage, and government training and apprenticeship pipelines built around those standards would weaken.

drawbacks.text: Davis-Bacon is the wage floor for laborers and mechanics on federally financed construction; repealing it removes the legal guarantee of locally prevailing pay for those workers [S2] [S3], and where local rates are below what federal projects pay, their earnings would drop.

The strongest good-faith argument for repeal is that prevailing wage rules raise the cost of federal construction projects, which taxpayers ultimately fund [S2]. An honest supporter should acknowledge that this saving comes directly out of construction workers' pay rather than out of anyone else's pocket.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward trade: lower labor costs for contractors (and possibly lower project costs for taxpayers) paid for out of construction workers' wages. Davis-Bacon's wage determinations are decades old and sometimes inaccurate, and compliance is a real burden, but the bill as written did not reform those flaws; it simply eliminated the wage floor. For ordinary working people the cost falls on the workers themselves, so the trade favors the companies doing the work.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Lee introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act in the Senate on January 30, 2017, joined by a list of Republican colleagues including Cruz, McCain, Cornyn, Scott, Flake, Perdue, Johnson, Alexander, and Rubio [S1] [S3].

The bill repeals the Davis-Bacon Act requirement that locally prevailing wages be paid on federally financed or assisted construction contracts, and nullifies references to those requirements in other laws [S2].
Twelve Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].

The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on January 30, 2017; the action history shows no further action, markup, or vote before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally funded projects kept the prevailing wage floor, and contractors who wanted to bid for public work using cheaper labor did not get the repeal they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Construction workers kept their wage floor

sides.party_line_note: All twelve cosponsors, including the sponsor, were Republicans, and the record shows no Democratic support; the bill never reached the floor for a vote [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Repeal would have let contractors on federally financed building and public works pay below the local prevailing wage, directly increasing their margins on public contracts at the expense of the workers they hire. The bill died, so nothing changed for them.

Davis-Bacon's prevailing wage floor is a core protection these trades rely on; repeal would have undercut union wage standards and the apprenticeship systems built on them. The bill never advanced, so the floor remains.
